t: Maximum Enemy Forts That Can Be Captured
o: You move an army from one of your forts (value 1) to an empty position (value -1), passing only over enemy forts (0), capturing all of them. Maximize captures. So we look for a maximal block of zeros with a 1 on one side and a -1 on the other; the block length is the capture count. In [1,0,0,-1,0,0,0,0,1]: the run of four zeros between the -1 at index 3 and the 1 at index 8 gives 4. If no such configuration exists, return 0. n ≤ 1000 makes even O(n²) fine, but a single pass over nonzero cells works.
k: Captures = length of a zero-run bordered by 1 on one side and -1 on the other.
Scan outward from every nonzero cell in both directions.

a.i: For every cell that is 1 or -1, walk left and right over zeros; if the walk terminates at the opposite kind of nonzero cell, the zero count is a candidate. Take the maximum.
s: For each nonzero forts[i], expand left counting zeros; if the boundary is the opposite sign, record the count.
a.t: O(n) amortized — each cell is scanned a constant number of times across all expansions

a.i: Walk once keeping the index of the previous nonzero cell. When hitting a new nonzero cell, if its sign differs from the previous one, the zeros strictly between them form a capturable run of length (cur − prev − 1). This directly enumerates all zero-runs bounded by unlike signs.
s: Keep prev = index of last nonzero cell (init -1).
At each nonzero cell with prev ≠ -1 and opposite sign, update ans with cur − prev − 1.

w: The one-pass previous-nonzero solution is the cleanest; the expansion version is easier to reason about. Edge cases: adjacent 1 and -1 with no zeros between captures 0; runs bounded by like signs (1…1 or -1…-1) don't count; no move possible → 0. Follow-up: what if the army could make multiple moves? Then it becomes a graph reachability question.
